http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/04/iran-.text: Iran announced that it would target any US warship that may try to impose a different route than the one that Tehran has allowed for ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz, Mohsen Rezaei, a senior advisor to Iran's supreme leader, said Monday."(We won't allow) the second corridor to open. Even if they (US) deploy warships, we will target them," Rezaei said in an interview with Iran's state media.Rezaei also warned of targeting US ships and bases if the country continued the naval blockade on Iran."There will certainly be serious dangers to the US ships and bases. We will not sit and watch the US continue the naval blockade," he added.While President Donald Trump said on Monday he expected negotiations to begin within the next day or two after threathening that newly planned talks with Tehran are the “last chance” for Iran to forge a deal before devastating strikes on the country, Iran immediatly denied holding new negotiations saying the Islamic Republic was only working out an agreement with Oman at the moment over a temporary route for shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.Foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei insisted the strait, the critical waterway where about a fifth of all traded oil and natural gas flowed before the start of the war, will "remain closed until US violations end".Cargo vessel hit by 'unknown projectile'Meanwhile, a cargo vessel in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Oman was struck by an "unknown projectile", a British maritime agency said on Tuesday, without giving specifics on damage or injuries.Authorities started an investigation into the vessel, which has not been named, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said, adding the incident occurred 37 kilometres northeast of Al Khasab, Oman.

https://malawi24.com/2026/09/03/malawi-m.text: MALAWI MINERALS TO CREATE JOBS IN POLAND Business September 03, 2026 04:43 AM Malawi24 Reporter Share …848 Billion Kwacha to be invested in Poland processing plant …Mkango scheme to spirit out Songwe rare earths …Mutharika’s Executive Order Number 2 thrown to the dogs âWhile millions of young people in Malawi are waking up daily to the harsh reality of unemployment and economic hardship, natural resources extracted from the local soil are positioned to drive high-tech industrial development and high-paying jobs over 8,000 kilometers away in Central Europe, Poland. âAccording to technical disclosures regarding the Songwe Hill Rare Earths project in Phalombe, operated by Canadian firm Mkango Resources through its local outfit, Lancaster Exploration, the local mine is set to offer local Malawians crumbs while the main steak is to be enjoyed overseas before powering industries in the US. âUnder the project structure disclosed by the developers, operations at the Songwe Hill site in Phalombe will be confined strictly to open-pit mining, crushing, flotation, and preliminary washing. âThese basic processes are only designed to extract an unrefined intermediate compound known as Mixed Rare Earth Carbonate (MREC). In an update published by the United States International Development Finance Corporation, âMkango will not be processing the compound in Malawi but will instead be shipping the unrefined substance to Mozambique before spiriting it out to PuÅawy, Poland, in Central Europe. â âIn PuÅawy, Mkango has partnered with Polish chemical giant Grupa Azoty to construct a state-of-the-art separation plant which is valued at US$ 212 million (about 848 billion Malawi Kwacha at the prevailing rate of MK4000 to 1 US$). âThis multi-billion facility in Poland is where the true value-addition, chemical refining, and high-tech separation of neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, and terbium will take place. âWhile Malawians might benefit some job opportunities from this arrangement, it will mostly be short-term roles created at the local extraction site in Phalombe that will predominantly consist of low-wage, physical labor. They are expected to be hired for basic site clearing, manual digging, security guarding, site driving, and low-level equipment maintenance. Poland, on the other hand, gets to benefit the true long-term industrial reward funded by natural resources dug out of Malawian earth. A mining expert who spoke on condition of anonymity told Malawi24 that âthe facility in Poland has the higher chances of generating hundreds of high-paying career opportunities for chemical engineers, metallurgists, specialized plant operators, and industrial lab technicians. 11 thoughts on “ MALAWI MINERALS TO CREATE JOBS IN POLAND ” That’s good that we malawians we have minerals but the sad part is we’re exploring our minerals to oversees of which we will not benefit much for this minerals only Malawian leaders and the investors they’re the ones who is going to benefits.Why don’t we refined our minerals at our own country? Wake up malawians. Reply This is a great exploitation to many Malawians. I hope our president will look into this again. The most benefited are the top officials, so how can you expect corruption to end, this is the effect of corruption in our mining sector. Reply Not good enough Malawi to send the Stuff abroad to be processed..Why not processing here?? Of course they can also creat jobs right here in Mw. Reply Very significant to the development of the country Reply If we were brave enough, this is not the time to exploit these minerals. We need stable power supply in abundance before we can see this unfair arrangement as unfair. We are determined not to develop ourselves as such it will be very difficult, even after a century from now, to truly benefit from what our Gods meant for us under our feet Reply This is a great news. I hope this project will change lives of many malawian for the better . Reply It’s unfortunate to hear that there is such level of exploitation. It’s stated and clear that this venture will benefit the polish government and people of Poland. Very sad and short sightediness of our government to enter into such an arrangement. If this is the sort of arrangement that will be there I am strongly advising that it should be stopped and abandoned. For how long shall we cerebrate being taken advantage of. Reply This arrangement has to be cancelled . Mineral purifying should be done in Malawi or else pack and go. Burkona Faso is doing the same. No unprocessed mi eral leaves the country. Reply Value addition has to be done here in Malawi, then we can build capacity Reply So how do stop this overexploitation of our minerals resources by selfish investors who care nothing about us? Photograph: snapshot-photography/F Boillot/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen A pro-Palestine demonstration in Berlin's Kreuzberg district, 7 October 2026. Photograph: snapshot-photography/F Boillot/Shutterstock European Union ‘Self-imposed irrelevance’: why the EU is failing to act on growing public criticism of Israel While Israel’s actions against Palestinians intensify public anger, the bloc remains paralysed along familiar fault lines Jennifer Rankin in Brussels Fri 9 Oct 2026 05.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 05.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google W hen the British government announced sweeping sanctions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements and condemned “ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank by state-backed “settler terrorists”, some EU diplomats hoped this dramatic shift in UK government policy towards Israel would have a galvanising effect on the rest of Europe. So far, it has not. Although France and Canada joined the UK in pledging to ban goods from illegal settlements and impose sanctions on “those who facilitate them or profit from them”, there has not yet been a wider ripple effect. A meeting of EU foreign affairs ministers on Monday is likely to showcase the bloc’s stasis in policy towards Israel – a stalemate that is at odds with rising public criticism in Europe of Israel’s government. A survey of 10 European countries, including Spain, France and Sweden, found large majorities of people had a negative opinion of Israel . Views had become more negative compared with the previous year, according to the Pew Research Center, mostly after the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, which unleashed a new crisis in the Middle East and a global economic shock. In Poland, negative views jumped eight points to 70% of respondents, in Italy they increased by nine points to 75% and in Germany they also rose by nine points to 73%. View image in fullscreen Buildings destroyed in Israeli military strikes on Gaza City. Photograph: Jehad Alshrafi/AP Israel is facing ever deeper isolation in the theatre of public opinion. Five countries chose to boycott the Eurovision song contest this year over Israel’s participation, after organisers declined to exclude it over its conduct in the Gaza war and rising violence in the West Bank. Organisers have now decided that broadcasters will no longer be eligible to host the song contest if their state is involved in an armed conflict or sensitive geopolitical situation. More than 74,000 people, including at least 21,200 children, have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its war in retaliation for the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, in which the terrorist group killed 1,209 people – including 36 children – and took 251 hostages, inflicting a nationwide trauma . Gaza remains a humanitarian catastrophe , with people facing acute shortages of water, nutritious food and medical equipment and medicines, while contending with disease, unemployment, economic collapse and the threat of death or injury. Israel’s airstrikes continue: the death toll includes 1,400 Palestinians killed since a ceasefire was declared a year ago. View image in fullscreen A commemorative installation on the beach in Tel Aviv, Israel, to mark the third anniversary of Hamas’s 7 October attack. Photograph: Jack Guez/AFP/Getty Images The EU talks on the Middle East will focus on the conflicts in Iran and Yemen, but ministers will also discuss the situation in Gaza and the West Bank in the context of elections in Israel on 27 October and the first legislative elections in Palestine in 20 years, which are expected by late November. The discussion is expected to expose familiar fault lines in the 27-member EU. One group of countries are vocal supporters of the Palestinian cause: Spain and Ireland were the first to call for a review of whether Israel’s conduct in the Gaza war was in breach of the human rights requirements of its association agreement with the EU, which covers the €68bn (£58bn) trade relationship, cooperation in research, environment and energy. A second group consistently opposes targeting Israel’s government: Germany and Austria are close allies for historical reasons, while Czechia and Italy are ideologically aligned with Benjamin Netanyahu’s administration. Among a third, larger group of countries in the middle are several, such as France and the Netherlands, that are increasingly critical of the Netanyahu government’s conduct in Gaza and its plans to build the vast E1 settlement , which threatens to critically damage the two-state solution. View image in fullscreen Benjamin Netanyahu speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations general assembly in New York last month. Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/AP Martin Konečný, the director of the Brussels-based European Middle East Project, thinks the EU has a diplomatic role to play as Israel advances with the controversial E1 plan. However, he does not see any sign of action. “The EU is basically staying in its usual self-imposed irrelevance,” he said. This is not an isolated view. More than 500 former senior EU officials and diplomats issued a statement this week condemning the bloc’s failure to take action over Israel’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank. The signatories, which include former prime ministers of France, Italy and Sweden, as well as Josep Borrell, the EU’s former chief diplomat, singled out Germany and Italy for the first time in stark, uncompromising language. “Germany and Italy continue to systematically block the adoption of any EU measures, thus becoming de facto complicit in undermining both EU values and the two-state solution,” wrote the group, which includes a few dozen senior figures from those two countries. Given their size, Germany and Italy have been crucial in preventing the EU from forging a weighted majority to impose trade sanctions and ban commerce with illegal settlements. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Michael Doyle, a former EU ambassador who co-organised the statement, told the Guardian the EU was not meeting the obligations of its treaties or international law. “Unfortunately our often-proclaimed EU values are set aside when it comes to the EU’s collective response to the dire plight of Palestinians,” he said. The widespread disquiet explained “why we get so many signatures from people who don’t normally sign such calls for action”. The statement was motivated by the absence of proposals from the European Commission, the guardian of EU law that initiates legislation for the 27-member bloc. The commission has declined to table proposals to ban trade with illegal settlements . The refusal to act has exasperated numerous lawyers and trade experts, who argue the ban is necessary for the EU to comply with a landmark advisory ruling from the international court of justice in 2024 on the illegality of the settlements. It told other countries to “take steps to prevent trade or investment relations that assists in the maintenance of the illegal situation created by Israel in the occupied Palestinian territory”. View image in fullscreen Ursula von der Leyen attends a joint debate before the EU summit in Strasbourg, France, later this month. Photograph: Pascal Bastien/AP Ursula von der Leyen, the commission’s president and a German Christian Democrat who is not afraid to take political risks, has argued the EU cannot act when member states disagree. In her annual state of the union speech last month, she lamented: “When Europe is divided, it cannot change the course of events.” A year earlier she presented proposals to suspend preferential trade with Israel but never found sufficient support from member states. Advocates of the EU taking a stronger approach are not convinced she cannot act. Konečný said: “It is not guaranteed that the qualified majority would be reached. But once the commission tables the proposal [on banning trade with settlements], that changes the dynamic.” View image in fullscreen Israeli flags outside the home and workplace of Mueyyid Hussein in Al-Lubban ash-Sharqiya, a village in the West Bank, 8 October 2026. Photograph: Issam Rimawi/Anadolu/Getty Images The blocking European governments may be lagging behind public opinion. Large majorities in Italy (88%) and Germany (83%) say they do not have confidence in Netanyahu “to do the right thing regarding world affairs”, according to the Pew Research Center ’s study. Meanwhile, the question of Israel-Palestine continues to roil the left. This week the Green party of England and Wales adopted a motion equating Zionism with racism , drawing widespread criticism. The motion from a small political party in the UK was strongly condemned by the head of the Jewish Greens in England and Wales (“ a very bad motion ”) and the European Greens, which stressed the importance of being “absolutely unambiguous” in the fight against antisemitism. Peace campaigners think it makes their job harder. The motion “hands ammunition to those who want to paint pro-Palestinian activism as illegitimate”, wrote Yachad, an organisation that seeks to build support among British Jews for a political resolution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Photograph: AAP/Supplied by Kevin Nguyen Melbourne Missing Australian hiker Jordan Yap last seen on remote trail found dead in Peru Family and friends say Melbourne man should be remembered for ‘immense joy he brought to so many people’s lives’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Guardian staff Sun 11 Oct 2026 03.45 EDT Last modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 04.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An Australian trekker who was last seen on a remote South American hiking trail has been found dead, his family have said. Jordan Yap, 30, last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek along Peru’s Huayhuash mountain range, 400km north-east of Lima. In a social media post on Saturday, his friends and family said “with a heavy heart we are sorry to tell you Jordan has been found, and he did not survive”. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “We want to thank everyone who has helped; friends and family, the contributors, the search teams, the police, the many groups we engaged with who gave their time and effort, everyone who helped to share on social media. We are appreciative of all of you. “Please remember Jordan as the vibrant man he was, and for the immense joy he brought to so many people’s lives. “Rest in peace Jordan – from your friends and family.” The Melbourne man was last seen near the beginning of his trek across the Cordillera Huayhuash circuit, which is regarded as a challenging, high-altitude trek through the remote Andes mountains. His friends and family regarded him as a very experienced hiker. His friends and family became concerned after he failed to make contact on his estimated return date, failed to check back into the Krusty hostel in Huaraz and missed a scheduled flight from Lima to Cusco. The avid trekker misplaced a satellite beacon he was travelling with days before he set off on the 120km hike, raising further concerns. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion A spokesperson from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade confirmed it was providing consular assistance to the family of an Australian who had died in Peru. “We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Kim Aris, the son of Myanmar's ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi, has long demanded ‘proof of life’ with regards to his mother. Photograph: Tian Macleod Ji/AP View image in fullscreen Kim Aris, the son of Myanmar's ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi, has long demanded ‘proof of life’ with regards to his mother. Photograph: Tian Macleod Ji/AP Myanmar Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi ‘sounds strong’ but is isolated, son says Kim Aris tells the Guardian chance to speak with detained Nobel laureate was ‘public relations’ move from military leaders Oliver Holmes in Bangkok Sat 24 Oct 2026 22.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 22.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Myanmar’s former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi appears to be in good physical and mental health but is living in near-complete isolation, her son has said after the first call with his 81-year-old mother in more than five years. “She still sounds certainly all there mentally, and physically she sounds strong,” Kim Aris said. “I don’t think she has anybody outside of the military or the police around her, so essentially she’s been held in solitary confinement from what I gather.” After being deposed in a 2021 military coup , the Nobel Peace prize laureate has been moved to an unspecified location in the capital. “I’m still not entirely sure where she is,” said Aris. “I think it’s a residence in Naypyidaw, which is fenced off and it has a scrubby bit of land around it.” View image in fullscreen Aung San Suu Kyi talks on the phone with her son on Thursday, in a photo released by the Myanmar presidential office. Photograph: Myanmar President Spokesperson Office/AP Aris, who has lived in the UK most of his life and whose late father was a British historian, was allowed to speak to his mother on Thursday at the Myanmar embassy in London . While he welcomed the chance to talk, he said the invitation was part of a “public relations” campaign by the country’s military leaders. The former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing has sought to rebuild international diplomatic ties, and in April switched his military fatigues for civilian clothes after elections that were widely condemned as a sham . Activists have long demanded “proof of life” for Aung San Suu Kyi, as well as scores of other political prisoners. In August, she was finally photographed during a Red Cross visit . Last week, a government spokesperson published images of her smiling in a wood-panelled room as officials delivered two gardening books given to her as gifts by Britain’s King Charles. A paper calendar on the wall behind her showed the date. Aris said these photo-ops were well-known stunts that the regime had used before to pretend his mother, a national icon, was being treated fairly. The daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San has spent much of her life since the late 1980s in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements. “She remains completely shut off from the rest of the world. I think she’s unaware of what’s happening outside of where she is because she’s not allowed any newspapers or radio or television,” Aris said. “She’s been locked up for five years on trumped-up, politically motivated charges and she should be free.” Ruled for decades by generals and suffering from western sanctions, Myanmar experienced a brief democratic moment after Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to run in a 2015 election that her party overwhelmingly won . She took up the role of “state counsellor” under a civilian-military power-sharing agreement. View image in fullscreen Aung San Suu Kyi shakes hands with Myanmar’s military commander-in-chief Min Aung Hlaing (left) in December 2015. Photograph: Lynn Bo Bo/EPA Her international reputation was soon tarnished after the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims . Aung San Suu Kyi flew to the international court of justice in The Hague, where she said she acknowledged military units might have used “disproportionate force”, but defended the government against accusations of genocide. Blunder in, abandon allies and court a dictator: it’s the Trump doctrine, now playing out in Myanmar | Steve Bloomfield Read more Aris said that his mother was never “silent” on the Rohingya crisis and what she said on the issue “could fill volumes”. Under her leadership, Myanmar launched a domestic inquiry and appointed the former UN chief Kofi Annan to head a commission. He added that as state counsellor, Aung San Suu Kyi was “always walking on a tightrope”, knowing the military could strip her of her fragile power at any moment. “The very hard-won nascent democracy that she was trying to lead was holding on to things by a thread,” he said. “The military could have taken over at any point, and they were doing their best to make my mother’s situation a lot more difficult and to undermine her position. And I think in that respect they did a pretty good job.” The 2021 power grab by the military triggered a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to conflict monitors. Aris said the level of public global support for his mother had “dwindled incredibly” since the Rohingya crisis and that the whole country was now suffering from a lack of international attention. While many governments have called for Aung San Suu Kyi’s release, she is not treated as the beloved international figure that she once was. “Never mind my mother, the fact that people ignore what’s happening in Burma shouldn’t be down to what was being done to the Rohingya,” he said, using the country’s former name. “And that seems to be the case sometimes, that people say: ‘Oh, well, look how the Rohingya were treated. We can ignore what’s happening in Burma.’” Explore more on these topics Myanmar Aung San Suu Kyi South and central Asia Myanmar coup Rohingya news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Aung San Suu Kyi’s son speaks to detained former Myanmar leader for first time in five years Myanmar’s ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi seen in rare photos after receiving gift from King Charles Red Cross visits Aung San Suu Kyi after Myanmar military pushed to prove she is alive Myanmar’s former leader Aung San Suu Kyi moved to house arrest in Naypyidaw Myanmar junta chief Min Aung Hlaing appointed president after ‘sham’ election Leaked footage and prison logs reveal Aung San Suu Kyi’s life in detention Myanmar junta to free about 6,000 prisoners in annual amnesty, including 180 foreigners Aung San Suu Kyi given partial pardon by Myanmar junta Villagers say 14 killed as Myanmar violence flares Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
